The Chamber of Hewn Stone was in the northeast of the courtyard, and had two entrances, one to the sacred area (the courtyard) and one to the non-sacred area, so half of it was sacred and half non-sacred (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17). The Sanhedrin sat in the part that was non-sacred, since sitting is forbidden in the sacred part (see also ibid. 7:6).

and when the row became corrupted. Murder cases multiplied and it became difficult to judge and punish all the murderers, so they exiled themselves from their place in order to remove from themselves the obligation to judge capital cases (see Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 8b).
and their last was Tiberias. The last place to which they were exiled was Tiberias. [Note: In the Commentary on the Mishnah Maimonides vocalizes the word 'Tiberias' as Teveryah.]
and tradition. Received tradition.
on condition that the Sanhedrin be ordained in the Land. That the judges of the Sanhedrin who judge outside the Land were ordained in the Land.
as we explained. Above 4:12.
they strip one liable to stoning of his clothes. In this way his death is quicker (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 6:3, based on Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 45a).

and a woman is not stoned naked but in one garment. When she is naked her disgrace is great, and it is better for her to suffer a slow death than to be disgraced (Babylonian Talmud, ibid.); and to prevent her disgrace it suffices that she wear one garment, and she need not remain in all her clothes (Mayim Chayim).
two heights. Twice the height of a person.
and he turns over and falls on his heart to the ground. The one being stoned who is pushed from behind falls with his chest toward the ground.
if he died from it, he is done. And there is no need to stone him with stones.
he shall surely be shot. Cast down.
the load of two people. That two people are needed to lift it because of its weight.

and the second witness lets go of his hand and throws the stone on his heart. Since it is too heavy for one person to carry, the two witnesses lift it together, and afterwards the second witness (who did not push the condemned at first) removes his hands from it and the other throws it on the one being stoned.
and if not, the stoning is by all Israel. The rest of the people throw stones at him until he dies.
but at the gate where he served. At the gate of the city where he worshiped, even if they tried him in another city.

and if it was a city most of whose inhabitants are gentiles, they stone him at the entrance of the court. Within the city, unlike other condemned persons whose place of execution must be distanced from the court (as explained above 12:3; for a similar law regarding the betrothed girl see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 3:9-11).
and this is a received tradition, etc.. That an idolater is stoned at the gate of the city where he worshiped.
up to his knees. Up to his knees, and they did this so that he would not move.

and they put a hard cloth inside the soft one. They press on his neck with a hard cloth so that he begins to choke and opens his mouth, but they wrap the hard one in a soft cloth so that his neck is not injured by the strangling (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 7:2).
they sever his head with the sword. They cut off his head with a sword.
in the manner that kings do. In the manner of the kings of the nations, who kill in this way.
and this one pulls toward himself and this one pulls toward himself. Two hold the ends of the cloth and each pulls the end in his hand until the condemned is strangled and dies.
to hang the blasphemer and the idolater. After they have been stoned.
the blasphemer. One who curses the Name is put to death by stoning (below halakhah 10).

'a curse of God is the hanged one'. The verse (Deuteronomy 21:23) refers to the law of hanging one who was put to death for his sin and the prohibition of leaving him overnight on the tree after hanging, and from it they derive that the executed person who is hanged is the one who cursed God.

and regarding an idolater it is said, 'he blasphemes the Lord'. So he too is called a blasphemer and must be hanged (for a comparison between the blasphemer and the idolater see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:6).
they sink the beam into the ground and the tree projects from it. They fix a beam in the ground, and from it extended a wooden pole on which they hung the one to be hanged.
and they bring his two hands together. They join and tie his two hands together, and they hang him by them on the tree (see Radbaz).
and if he stayed overnight. If he remained hanging at night.

rather, anyone who leaves his dead overnight transgresses a negative commandment. The prohibition "you shall not leave his body overnight" is not limited to those executed by the court but applies to any dead person (see also Hilchot Evel 4:9).
on a detached one. A tree that was planted in the ground and then uprooted.

so that it not require cutting, since the tree on which he is hanged is buried with him. The Torah wrote of the hanged one "you shall bury him," and since the tree too requires burial with him, it too must be in a state in which it can be buried immediately without further action (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 6:6).
in the vicinity of the executed. In the area adjacent to him.
one who has relations with his mother... and the woman who brings the animal upon herself. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:4.
his father's wife. Even if she is not his mother.
and his daughter-in-law. His son's wife.

and a betrothed girl. One who has relations with a virgin girl after she was betrothed to a man and before she entered the chuppah (ibid. 3:4). But if she was a minor or an adult woman, or had already had relations, or had entered the chuppah, one who has relations with her is liable to strangulation like one who has relations with a married woman.
and the blasphemer. One who curses the Lord (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:6).
and the idolater. Ibid. 3:1.
and one who gives of his seed to Molech. An idolatrous rite that includes passing a son through a fire (ibid. 6:3).
and a medium (ba'al ov). One who performs various acts that cause voices of supposed dead people to be heard (ibid. halakhah 1).
and a necromancer (ba'al yidoni). One who performs various acts that enable him to supposedly foretell the future (ibid. halakhah 2).
and the inciter. Of others to worship idols, even though he himself did not worship (ibid. 5:1).
and the one who leads astray. One who persuades the people of his city to worship idols, and the townspeople did worship (ibid. 4:1).
and the sorcerer. One who performs an act of sorcery (ibid. 11:15).
and one who desecrates the Sabbath. Hilchot Shabbat 1:1.
and one who curses his father or mother. Hilchot Mamrim 5:1.

and the rebellious son. A son who does not obey his father and mother, who under certain conditions is liable to stoning after stealing money from his parents and eating and drinking with it gluttonously (ibid. 7:1).

a priest's daughter who committed adultery while married. Although the usual death for a married woman is strangulation, the death of a priest's daughter is burning, while her paramour is liable to strangulation like other paramours of a married woman (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:6).
and one who has relations with his daughter... and his wife's mother's mother. Ibid. halakhah 5.

and this is when he had relations with them during his wife's lifetime, etc.. All of his wife's relatives mentioned here are forbidden under the penalty of karet even after his wife's death, but he is not liable to the court's death penalty for them after she died.
those executed. By the sword.
the murderer. Hilchot Rotzeach 1:1.
and the led-astray one. Each of the people of an apostate city who was led astray and worshiped idols (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:1).
one who has relations with a married woman. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:6.
and one who wounds his father or mother. Hilchot Mamrim 5:5.
and one who kidnaps an Israelite. And sells him after using him (Hilchot Genevah 9:1).
and a rebellious elder. A judge who disputes the Sanhedrin and rules that people should act according to his words (Hilchot Mamrim 3:5).
and the false prophet. One who prophesies something he did not hear, or says that something said to his fellow was said to him (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 5:8).
and one who prophesies in the name of an idol. Ibid. halakhah 6.
and although lashes are by three. Judges (above 5:4).
it stands in place of death. Lashes are considered a severe punishment and are a substitute for death, and one liable to karet who is flogged is released from his karet (below 17:7).
they flog in our times. Although the Temple is destroyed and the Sanhedrin does not sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone and capital cases cannot be judged (above 14:11).
judges outside the Land. Who are not ordained.
a rebuke-beating. Lashes by rabbinic enactment for those who commit prohibitions (see below 18:5).
with witnesses and warning. That two witnesses saw him commit the transgression and before he did so warned him not to do it and that if he does he will be flogged (see above 12:2).
and they examine the witnesses with inquiry and cross-examination. A thorough investigation of the details of the event they testify about.
as is done in capital cases. Above 12:3.

he transgressed a negative commandment that was converted into a positive one. A negative commandment where there is an explicit command to rectify the transgression by a specific act, so that the prohibition is converted into a positive commandment. One is not flogged for a negative commandment that is converted into a positive one, but if it is no longer possible to fulfill the positive commandment, one is flogged for it (below 18:2).

for although the warning is in doubt, since if he fulfills it he will be exempt. For at the time they warn him they cannot know with certainty whether he will transgress and be flogged, since he may fulfill the positive commandment and be exempt.
lashes and the court's death penalty together. That in a single act he transgresses two prohibitions, one for which he is liable to death and the other to lashes.

who slaughtered it and its offspring for idolatry. Slaughter is one of the services which, when done for idolatry, makes one liable to stoning (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 3:3). Also, it is forbidden to slaughter an animal and its offspring on the same day, and if he slaughtered, he is liable to lashes (Hilchot Shechitah 12:1). So one who slaughters an animal and its offspring on the same day for idolatry is liable by his slaughter to both death and lashes.
and if they warned him for lashes only. They warned him that if he transgresses he will be flogged, and did not say he would be put to death (see also ibid. halakhah 7).
at the time of the act. That two witnesses testify that he committed the forbidden act.

the prohibition itself is established by one witness. It is enough that one witness testifies that the thing is forbidden, and it will be possible to flog on his testimony if a person transgresses the prohibition before two witnesses.
the fat of the kidneys. One of the forbidden fats (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 7:7).
this is the produce of a vineyard planted with mixed species. Grain, vegetables, or grapes that grew in a vineyard sown with mixed species, and one who eats them is flogged (ibid. 10:6-7).
this woman is divorced or a zonah. And is forbidden to a priest, and if he married her he is flogged for relations with her (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:2).
even though the main prohibition is by one witness. Although it is known on the testimony of only one witness that the thing is forbidden (see also ibid. 1:22, Hilchot Shegagot 3:2).
he binds both his hands to the pillar, back and forth. They would lean the one being flogged against a low pillar and tie his two hands on both sides of the pillar.
and the synagogue attendant. The congregation's sexton, the officer who serves as the judges' agent to administer the lashes.
he holds his clothes... until he exposes his heart. So that the shoulders and chest are bare.
and the stone is placed behind him. Behind the one being flogged stood a stone on which the one administering the lashes stood, striking from behind and from a height.
and a strap of calf leather. Of calf hide.

doubled into two and two into four. They fold the strap in two and then double it again, or it means that they cut the folded strap into two (see the various explanations in the commentators on Mishnah Makkot 3:12 and on the Gemara there 22b).

and two straps of donkey leather go up and down in it. Within the folds of the calf straps, or at their sides, hung two straps of donkey hide, and these straps went up and down together with the calf straps during the beating (see further explanations in the commentators there).

and its length is such that it reaches the opening of his belly. The strap had to reach the navel of the one being flogged, and to fit the strap's length to the person being flogged they would thread the straps through a hole in the handle and shorten or lengthen it as needed (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makkot 3:13).
the man who strikes must be more knowledgeable and less strong. So that he does not strike very hard blows.
between his breasts. On the chest.
bent. Stooped.
and the judge shall cause him to lie down. For the term 'falling' is sometimes interpreted as bending (see Ketav VeHaKabbalah, Deuteronomy 25:2).
and he shall strike him before him. The one being flogged must be before him, in such a way that he sees him.
and he shall strike him: from here, we do not flog two at once. For it is written 'and he shall strike him' in the singular.

and he intends to finish the verses together with the lashes. He sets the pace of his reading according to the number of lashes so that he will finish reading at the time they end (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makkot 3:14).
and if he did not finish. The one striking, striking him at the time the reader finished reading.

as long as he strikes, he strikes on his word. Although the number of lashes he will receive was fixed in advance (below 17:1-2), the attendant may strike only on the direct instruction of the judge for each and every blow (so that if the judge notices that the one being flogged weakened in the middle of the beating he will not tell him to strike; Tiferet Yisrael, Makkot 3:14, and see below 17:2).
if he died under his hand, he is exempt. From exile for killing him (for one who kills while performing a commandment does not go into exile; Hilchot Rotzeach 5:6).
and if he added one strap beyond the estimate. If he struck with the strap one more time than the lashes that the judges estimated the one flogged could bear.
and the same applies to anyone who strikes his fellow, etc.. See also Hilchot Chovel 5:1.

even if he struck a slave... he is flogged. The prohibition of striking an Israelite includes also the prohibition of striking a Canaanite slave, since he is obligated in some of the commandments (ibid. halakhah 3).
a person does not both pay and receive lashes, as we have explained in several places. When he is liable to pay, he is not flogged (Hilchot Sechirut 11:1, 12:3; and see below 18:2).
according to his strength. The number of lashes that by estimate he is able to bear and remain alive (the estimate is made by those expert in the matter; Commentary on the Mishnah, Makkot 3:10).
as it is said, 'according to his wickedness, by number'. That the number of lashes should be according to his strength for his wickedness (see Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 3:10-11).

for if he adds one to him, it turns out that he struck him only the forty that were due him. So that even if by mistake he strikes one extra lash, he will not exceed the quota of lashes. But if he were striking him forty and by mistake added another lash, he would transgress "he shall not add" (Emek HaMelech, Ma'aseh Rav, Rashash, and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Makkot 3:10).
that are fit to be divided into thirds. A number of lashes that can be divided by three.

they estimated for him today that they would flog him twelve, and they did not flog him until tomorrow. An estimate for a particular day is not canceled the next day, and no lashes beyond those set by the first estimate are added.

they estimated that he would be flogged tomorrow twelve, and he was not flogged until the third day. An estimate from one day to the next still counts as an estimate, but on the third day from the estimate it is canceled and he is flogged according to the new estimate (Arukh HaShulchan 56:9, Yad Peshutah). Some explain that in any case where the estimate was not made for that day (even if made for the following day), it is canceled, and he is flogged more if they estimate him for more (Kesef Mishneh, Shalal David).

if they estimated him with one estimate, he is flogged and exempt. If they estimated that he can receive lashes for all the liabilities he incurred (for example, he can receive the full forty lashes for one liability and at least some of the lashes for the second liability), he is flogged all at once.

and if not, he is flogged, heals, and is flogged again. If he cannot receive more than forty lashes at one time, he is flogged for one liability as much as he can bear, and after he recovers he is flogged again for the remaining liabilities for which he is liable to lashes.
he can receive forty-five. For the two liabilities for lashes.
he soiled himself. His orifices opened.
that he was disgraced. He was humiliated.

even if he soiled himself from the time he left the court to be flogged, etc.. Even if he already soiled himself when he was being taken out to be flogged (and not only right at the time of the beating), one might have thought that since he has great fear of the lashes he should not be flogged at all (Lechem Mishneh, Mishneh LaMelech).
and even from the evening. For example, they estimated him to be flogged the next day, and already in the evening before that he soiled himself.
they estimated him for two floggings. That he incurred two liabilities for lashes and they estimated that he be flogged for both together (as above halakhah 4).

and he was flogged and soiled himself, whether in the first or the second, he is exempt. Even if he soiled himself during the lashes for the first transgression, by his soiling he is exempt also from the second lashes.
the strap broke. The strap with which he is flogged was cut.

if it broke during the first, he is exempt from the first flogging and is flogged the second estimate. When the strap broke and it is not possible to continue flogging, the one liable is exempt from the series of lashes he is receiving now. But since he was not 'disgraced,' he is not entirely exempt from the liability for lashes, and he must continue to be flogged the series of lashes for the second transgression.

they bound him to the pillar to be flogged, and he cut the ropes and fled. They tied him to the pillar to which the one flogged is attached (above 16:8) and he cut the ropes and fled; since he was disgraced by this, he is considered already 'disgraced' and is exempt from lashes (see Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 28a and Rashi there).
he returns to his validity. And becomes valid as a witness (Hilchot Edut 12:4).
once he was flogged. Immediately after he was flogged.
only those liable to karet. Whose karet carries no liability to the court's death penalty, and who are to be flogged (below 18:1).
are released from their karet. Provided they repent along with the lashes (Commentary on the Mishnah, Makkot 3:1, 3:15).

a high priest who sinned is flogged by three like the rest of the people. Unlike capital cases, where his law differs from the rest of the people and he is judged by a court of seventy-one (above 5:1, and see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:22).
and he returns to his greatness. For the sanctity of the high priest is not nullified (see Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 2:1).
head of the academy. The head of the court of seventy-one, the president of the Sanhedrin.

for we raise in holiness and do not lower. Since he was flogged he cannot serve as head of the academy, but since he was already head of the academy he is not to be appointed as an ordinary judge (see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:21).
for which one is liable to karet and which has no death penalty of the court. But those liable to the court's death penalty, though there is karet in them, are not flogged (below halakhah 2).
such as one who eats forbidden fat, etc.. Below 19:1-2 the negative commandments that carry karet and those that carry the court's death penalty are detailed.
one who eats tevel. Grain from which terumot and ma'aserot have not been separated.
one who wears shaatnez. A garment made of wool and linen together.
but a negative commandment that involves no action. That is, one done by speech, hearing, or thought.
a talebearer. One who peddles information about people or their actions; this prohibition also includes the prohibition of speaking slander (Hilchot De'ot 7:1-2).
and one who takes vengeance. Against his fellow, for example refusing to lend to his fellow because the fellow had not lent to him earlier (ibid. halakhah 7).
and one who bears a grudge. Who keeps resentment even though he does not take revenge (ibid. halakhah 8).
one who bears a false report. A judge who hears the words of one litigant in the absence of the other (below 21:7).
one who swears. A false oath (Hilchot Shevuot 1:3) or a vain oath (ibid. halakhah 7).

and one who substitutes. One who makes a substitution, saying that an ordinary animal shall be in place of a consecrated animal. It is forbidden by Torah law to substitute, and one who substitutes is flogged (Hilchot Temurah 1:1).
and one who curses his fellow by the Name. By one of the names of God or by a substitute name (below 26:3).

a negative commandment given as a warning of the court's death penalty. A prohibition written in the Torah for the purpose of warning of the court's death penalty. Since the main point of the prohibition relates to the penalty of death and not to lashes, even if he transgressed in a way that does not make him liable to death (for example, if they warned him of lashes and not of death, or if he transgressed in a way that does not carry death), he is not flogged for this prohibition.

and any negative commandment given for payments... one is not flogged for it. A prohibition for which one is liable to pay money is not punished by lashes, but he pays the money (although when he does an act that carries liability to lashes, and in addition is liable for this act to payments for another reason, he is flogged and does not pay; see Hilchot Genevah 3:1).

you shall not steal. The wording here is as in the Ten Commandments. However, that prohibition was stated regarding kidnapping (see Hilchot Genevah 9:1), so it seems the intent is the prohibition "you shall not steal" in the portion of Kedoshim (Leviticus 19:11), from which the prohibition of stealing money is learned (see Hilchot Genevah 1:1).

a negative commandment that is converted into a positive one. A negative commandment where there is an explicit command to rectify the transgression by a specific act, so that it is converted into a positive commandment.
you shall not take the mother with the young. From the nest; and if he took, he is commanded by the positive commandment "you shall surely send away the mother" (Deuteronomy 22:7).

you shall not finish the corner of your field. That he not reap the whole field for himself but leave a corner for the poor; and if he reaped it, he is commanded by the positive commandment "for the poor and the stranger you shall leave them" (Leviticus 19:10), to give the poor from what he reaped.

one is not flogged for it unless he did not fulfill the positive commandment in it. If the positive commandment in the prohibition became void and can no longer be fulfilled (for example, the mother bird died, or the harvest was lost), he is flogged (see Hilchot Shechitah 13:1, Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 1:2-3).
and for any general negative commandment one is not flogged. As explained in the next halakhah.
and for all other negative commandments in the Torah one is flogged. For their enumeration see below 19:4.
what is a general negative commandment, etc.. Two kinds of negative commandments are defined as general ones, as explained here.

one negative commandment that includes many matters, such as 'You shall not eat over the blood'. That in one warning of the Torah several unrelated things are prohibited. In this example, "you shall not eat over the blood," many prohibitions are included, among them: the prohibition of eating from an animal before its life has left it (Hilchot Shechitah 1:2), the prohibition of providing the mourners' meal for those executed by the court, and the prohibition on judges eating on the day they put someone to death (above 13:4). Since all these prohibitions are included in one warning, one is not flogged for them.

and likewise if it is said, etc.. The second type of general prohibition is where the Torah explicitly writes several prohibitions but does not give a separate warning for each, and includes them all in one warning.
one is not flogged for each one. If he transgressed several of these prohibitions together, he is not flogged for each prohibition separately, but flogged only once for all of them.
unless he divided them into other negative commandments. That the Torah prohibited some of the prohibitions included in this warning separately elsewhere.
or it was said from tradition that they are divided. It was learned by tradition that one is flogged for each of the prohibitions included in this warning.
do not eat of it raw or boiled in water. The prohibition of eating the Passover offering (which must be eaten roasted) boiled, or roasted a little so that it is not yet fit for eating.
he is not flogged for the raw and the boiled separately. Even if he ate both raw and boiled, he receives one set of lashes (see also Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:4).
and new grain. The prohibition of eating from the new grain before the omer offering is brought on the 16th of Nisan (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:2).
and parched grain. Roasted wheat kernels.
and fresh ears. Moist wheat kernels.

and he made him liable for three lashes for the three; from tradition they learned that this is to divide. Although all three are included in one warning, it was learned by tradition that one is flogged for each of them separately, and if he ate bread, parched grain, and fresh ears before the omer was brought, he is flogged three sets of lashes (ibid. halakhah 3).

for it is said, 'There shall not be found among you one who makes his son or daughter pass through fire, one who practices divination, etc.'. And it continues, "a soothsayer, a diviner, a sorcerer, one who casts spells, one who consults a ghost or a familiar spirit, or one who inquires of the dead" (Deuteronomy 18:10-11). Although the Torah included many prohibitions in the warning "there shall not be found among you," one is flogged for each separately, because two of these prohibitions (soothsayer and diviner) were prohibited with a separate warning elsewhere.

if he ate forbidden fat a third time, they do not flog him, etc.. A person who willfully transgresses a prohibition carrying karet is basically liable to death, though his death is left to Heaven; but when he abandons himself to the same transgression time after time, they hasten his death (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 81b).
and they give him bread of adversity and water of affliction. A limited amount of food and drink (based on Isaiah 30:20).
until his belly bursts. And he dies.
they do not kill him, as we explained. That they do not kill unless he explicitly consigns himself to death and says, 'I do this on that condition' (above 12:2).
and they do not flog him. For lashes too require a warning, and they do not flog without warning (above 16:4).
if he returned a third time and transgressed and they warned him, etc.. Since he transgresses time after time transgressions that carry death, they hasten his death.
and all those who did not accept the warning, they give them a rebuke-beating. Already the first and second time.
a rebuke-beating. Lashes by rabbinic enactment.
and one who curses by a soothsayer. One who curses the name of God by the name of an idol (see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:9).

and one who has relations with a gentile woman. One who has relations with a gentile. This law applies when he does so publicly before ten Israelites, and only at the time of the act; after he separated, it is forbidden for zealots to harm him (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 12:4-5).

the court does not deal with them, but the zealots strike them. For they are not liable to the court's death penalty for these acts. Nevertheless, an individual who is zealous for God's honor may kill them.
and anyone who kills them is meritorious. The act of killing them is proper and praiseworthy, as the Torah praised Pinchas who killed Zimri (see Numbers 25:1-15).
a priest who served in a state of impurity. And became liable to death at the hands of Heaven (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:1).
his fellow priests did not bring him to court. To punish him with lashes as he deserves by law.
young priests. Young priests.
they take him outside the courtyard and smash his brains with clubs. See also ibid. halakhah 2.

for the court does not put anyone to death or flog on the basis of his own confession. Unlike monetary cases, where a person is held liable on his admission, in capital cases and cases of lashes one is not punished on the basis of a person's confession.
for Joshua killed Achan. Who confessed that he had misappropriated from the ban of Jericho (see Joshua 7:20-25).
and David the Amalekite convert. Who confessed that he killed Saul (see II Samuel 1:10-15).
it was a ruling for the hour. And we do not learn from it for later generations.
or it was the law of kingship. That a king may kill for the repair of the world and the need of the hour (Hilchot Melachim 3:10).
lest his mind became deranged over this matter. That when he wants to die because of madness he will claim that he sinned and is liable to death.
the toilers, the bitter of soul, who long for death. People who spend all their days in toil or are so depressed that they despise life and wait for death (based on Job 3:20-21).
who are always thrusting swords into their bellies and throwing themselves, etc.. They try to commit suicide at every opportunity.
and the rule of the matter is that it is a decree of the King. Although various reasons were brought here for the matter, the main point is that this law is a scriptural decree.
(1-7) one who has relations with his sister... and with a niddah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:7.
(8) one who eats forbidden fat. Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 7:1.
(9) one who eats blood. Ibid. 6:1.
(10) one who eats chametz on Passover. Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 1:1.
(11) one who eats on Yom Kippur. Hilchot Shevitat Asor 1:4.
(12) one who does work on Yom Kippur. Ibid. halakhah 1.
(13) one who eats notar. Meat of sacrifices after the time for eating them has passed (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:10).
(14) one who eats piggul. Meat of a sacrifice that was intended to be offered or eaten after its proper time ('intention outside its time,' ibid. halakhah 6).
(15) an impure person who ate sacred meat. An impure person who ate the meat of a sacrifice (ibid. halakhah 13).
(16) an impure person who entered the Temple courtyard. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:12.
(17) one who slaughters sacrifices outside. Outside the courtyard (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 18:3).
(18) one who offers sacrifices outside. One who brings up and offers a sacrifice on an altar outside the courtyard (ibid. halakhah 2).
(19) one who compounds the oil. One who makes oil in the formula of the anointing oil in order to anoint with it (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:4).
(20) one who anoints with the anointing oil. That Moses our teacher made (ibid. halakhah 5).
(21) one who compounds the incense. One who makes incense in the formula of the Temple's incense of spices in order to smell it (ibid. 2:9).

(1-2) a non-priest who ate great terumah... and a non-priest who ate terumat ma'aser. A person who is not a priest who ate from the great terumah that is separated from the crop and given to priests, or from terumat ma'aser that is separated from the Levites' tithe and given to a priest (Hilchot Terumot 6:5-6, 10:4).

(3) a non-priest who ate bikkurim after they entered Jerusalem. Bikkurim are the first fruits of the seven species brought to the priest in the Temple; they are called 'terumah' and have the law of terumah (Hilchot Bikkurim 3:1).
(4) a non-priest who ate challah. That is separated from the dough and given to the priest, is called 'terumah' and has the law of terumah (Hilchot Terumot 10:4).

(5) one who eats tevel from which great terumah and terumat ma'aser were not separated. Food from which one must separate terumot and ma'aserot, before they have been separated (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:19).
(6) one who eats from dough from which challah was not separated. Hilchot Bikkurim 8:5.
(7) an impure priest who ate pure terumah. Hilchot Terumot 7:1.
(8) a priest who entered the Holy of Holies not for service. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:3.
(9) a priest who left the Temple during service. In the middle of serving (ibid. halakhah 5).
(10) a Levite who performed the service of the priests. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 3:11.
(11) a non-priest who served in the Temple. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 9:1.
(12) one lacking garments. A priest who lacks one of the priestly garments.
he is like a non-priest and is flogged if he served. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 10:4.
(13) an impure priest who served. Who served in the Temple (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:1).
(14) a drunk who served. Ibid. 1:1.
(15) a tevul yom who served. An impure person who immersed is still considered impure until evening and is forbidden to serve in the Temple (ibid. 4:4).
(16) one lacking atonement. A zav, zavah, woman after childbirth, or metzora who became pure from their impurity but have not yet brought the offering that completes their purification process.

who served. In Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash (ibid.) he wrote that although he is forbidden to serve, if he served he is exempt from death and lashes. Therefore some wrote that there is a scribal error here and it should read 'with extra garments who served' (a priest who served wearing a garment in addition to the priestly garments, for example an ordinary priest who served wearing eight garments or a priest who served wearing two sashes, etc.; Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 10:5) instead of 'one lacking atonement who served' (Kesef Mishneh and others). Others wrote that he retracted (Arukh HaShulchan 60:14, R. Y. Kafih).
(17) one with unshorn hair who served. A priest with overgrown hair (whose hair grew for at least thirty days) who serves in the Temple (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 1:8).
(18) one with torn garments who served. One who serves in the Temple wearing torn garments (ibid. halakhah 14).

one who serves without sanctifying hands and feet, etc.. Priests are commanded to wash their hands and feet before beginning service in the Temple, and a priest who served without washing is liable to death. However, one is not flogged for this since it is a positive commandment.
a prophet who suppressed his prophecy. Who did not prophesy the prophecy he was told to prophesy.
even though all three are liable to death. Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 9:2-3.
for they come from a general positive commandment. Their prohibition is not stated explicitly in negative language but is learned from the implication of the command in positive language.

and a negative commandment that comes from a positive one is like a positive commandment. Such a prohibition is not considered a negative commandment but a positive one (see also Hilchot Ishut 1:8, Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:8 and others).
(166) a king who multiplied wives. Who married more than eighteen wives (Hilchot Melachim 3:2).
(167) a king who multiplied silver and gold. To put in his treasuries and take pride (ibid. 3:4).
(168) a king who multiplied horses. Beyond what is needed for his chariot (ibid. 3:3).
their mnemonic is YiLKU ZeDIM. This is the numerical value of the number of those flogged.
(1) one who makes an image. A form for the sake of idolatry (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 3:9).
(2) one who makes a form for ornament. Even if not for idolatry (ibid. 3:10).

(3) one who turns to idols by one of the acts. Who turns toward idolatry, for example by reading books that explain the ways of its worship or looking at its image, provided he turned toward it in a way that involves an act (ibid. 2:2-3).
(4) one who sets up a pillar. A structure used for worship (ibid. 6:6).
(5) one who plants a tree in the Temple. In the whole area of the courtyard (ibid. 6:9).
(6) one who places a figured stone. A decorated stone that was placed before an idol to bow upon (ibid. 6:6).
(7-8) one who vows in the name of an idol, one who swears by it. So that the gentile will believe him (ibid. 5:10).
(9) one who derives benefit from it. One who benefits from idolatry or from the vessels used in it or from the things offered to it (ibid. 7:2).
(10) one who builds an apostate city. A city whose majority of inhabitants were led astray by some of its people to worship idols; it is burned and forbidden to rebuild (ibid. 4:8).
(11) one who benefits from an apostate city. From its property, which is to be burned (ibid. 4:7).
(12) one who follows the customs of the gentiles. Who imitates them in dress or hair style and the like (ibid. 11:1).
(13) the soothsayer. One who performs various acts and says what will happen (ibid. 11:7).
(14) the augurer. One who reads the stars (ibid. 11:9).
(15) the diviner. One who decides what to do according to various signs (ibid. 11:4).
(16) the charmer. One who speaks meaningless words and imagines that they are of benefit (ibid. 11:10).
(17) one who inquires of the dead. Who performs various acts to cause the dead to appear to him (ibid. 11:13).
(18) one who erases a Name. Of the names of God (Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:1).

and similarly, such as one who demolishes a stone from the altar or burns wood from the Temple. Just as it is forbidden to erase the Name, so it is forbidden to perform acts of destruction and damage to the altar and the Temple (ibid. halakhah 7, Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 1:17).
(19) one who extinguishes the fire of the altar. Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:6.
(20) one who goes up on it by steps. Who ascends the altar by steps and not by the ramp (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 1:17).
(21) one who enters the courtyard in impure garments. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:16.

(22) a zav and the like who entered the Temple Mount. The impurity of a zav is more severe than that of other impure people, so he is forbidden to enter the area of the Temple Mount and not only the courtyard (ibid. halakhah 8).
(23) one who removes the poles of the ark. Who removes from the Ark of the Covenant its carrying poles (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 2:13).
(24) one who detaches the breastplate from the ephod. Who separates the breastplate's attachment from the ephod (ibid. 9:10).
(25) one who tears the opening of the robe. Who tears the neck opening of the high priest's robe, and the same applies to one who tears any priestly garment in a destructive manner (ibid. 9:3).
(26) one who offers on the golden altar. The inner altar in the sanctuary, intended only for burning incense. If he offered anything else on it he is flogged (ibid. 2:11).
(27) a priest who entered the sanctuary not at the time of service. It is permitted to enter the sanctuary only for service or prostration (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:4).
(28) a blemished priest who entered there. The sanctuary; and he is forbidden to enter even from the altar onward toward the sanctuary (ibid. 6:1).
(29) a drunk who entered there. Ibid. 1:16.
(30) a blemished priest who served. A priest with an external physical blemish who served in the Temple (ibid. 6:1).
(31) an uncircumcised man who served. An uncircumcised priest who served in the Temple (ibid. 6:8).
(32) a priest who performed the service of the Levites. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 3:11.
(33) a priest who entered the Temple with unshorn hair. With overgrown hair (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 1:15).
(34) a priest who entered the Temple with torn garments. Ibid.
(35) one who consecrates blemished animals. An animal with an external physical blemish (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:2).
(36-38) one who slaughters them, one who sprinkles their blood, one who burns their sacrificial parts. Ibid. 1:4.
(39) one who offers gentiles' blemished sacrifices. Ibid. 1:6.
(40) one who inflicts a blemish on sacrificial animals at the time of the Temple. And even nowadays he transgresses a prohibition, but is not flogged (ibid. 1:7).
(41-42) one who works with sacrificial animals, one who shears them. Who does work with a sacrificial animal or shears its wool (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:7).
(43) one who burns leaven or honey. On the altar as an offering or with an offering (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:1).

(44) one who makes the remainders of meal offerings leavened. The meal offerings brought to the altar are made of matzah and not leavened, and even their remainders eaten by the priests must remain matzah and not be leavened (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:14).
(45) one who offers without salt. It is forbidden to offer sacrifices on the altar without salting (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:12).
(46) one who offers a harlot's fee. Who offers a sacrifice from an animal that a harlot received for her act of harlotry.
or a dog's price. The payment received for the sale of a dog (ibid. 3:7).

(47-50) one who puts oil on a sinner's meal offering... one who puts frankincense on it. Oil and frankincense are put on all meal offerings, except a meal offering brought as a sin offering and the sotah's meal offering, on which it is forbidden to put oil and frankincense (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:8, Hilchot Sotah 3:13).
(51) one who separates the head of a bird sin offering. In the pinching of a bird sin offering, the bird's head is not to be separated from its body (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:6).
(52) one who substitutes for altar sacrifices. One who makes a substitution, saying that an ordinary animal shall be in place of a consecrated animal (Hilchot Temurah 1:1).
(53) one who eats sacred meat that became impure. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:12.
(54) one who eats from disqualified sacrifices. One who eats from a sacrifice that was disqualified (ibid. halakhah 3).
(55) a priest who ate the meat of most-holy sacrifices outside the courtyard. For the meat of most-holy sacrifices is eaten by priests and only in the courtyard (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:5).
(56) a non-priest who ate the meat of most-holy sacrifices after the sprinkling of the blood. Ibid. halakhah 8.
(57) a non-priest who ate the meat of a firstborn. The firstborn of a pure animal is given to priests, offered as a sacrifice, and eaten by them in Jerusalem (Hilchot Bechorot 1:16).

(58) a priest's daughter who married a non-priest and ate the breast and thigh, etc.. The breast and thigh are portions of the peace offerings given to the priests and eaten also by their sons and wives. If a priest's daughter married a non-priest she is forbidden to eat the breast and thigh even if her non-priest husband died and she has no son by him (although in that case she is permitted to eat terumah again; Hilchot Terumot 6:7).
(59) a challalah who ate terumah. A priest's daughter who had relations with a man forbidden to her and became a challalah or a zonah is forbidden to eat terumah (ibid.).
(60) one who eats lesser sacrifices before the sprinkling of the blood. Only after the sprinkling of the blood is the meat of the sacrifices permitted for eating (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:4).
(61) one who eats sacrifices outside Jerusalem. Lesser sacrifices, which are eaten anywhere in Jerusalem (ibid. halakhah 5).
(62) one who eats a firstborn outside Jerusalem. Hilchot Bechorot 1:16.
(63) one who eats second tithe outside Jerusalem after it has seen the face of the House. One who eats outside Jerusalem second tithe that was in the city and left it (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:5).

(64-65) a priest who ate bikkurim after they entered Jerusalem before they were set down in the courtyard, a priest who ate bikkurim outside Jerusalem after they were set down in the courtyard. The bikkurim are brought to the priest in the courtyard and set down there; before that the priest is forbidden to eat them, and afterwards he must eat them in Jerusalem (Hilchot Bikkurim 3:3).

(66) one who eats in Jerusalem second tithe that became impure before it was redeemed. Second tithe is eaten only in purity, and if it became impure it is redeemed and becomes ordinary food, and only then is it permitted to eat (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:1).
(67) an impure person who ate pure second tithe in Jerusalem. Ibid.
(68) one who eats second tithe in aninut. While he is an onen, on the day of his relative's death (ibid. 3:5).
and likewise all sacrifices. Eaten in aninut (ibid. 3:7).

(69) an uncircumcised man who ate sacred meat. A man who is not circumcised who ate the meat of the Passover offering or other sacrifices (Hilchot Korban Pesach 9:8, and see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:9).
or terumot. Hilchot Terumot 7:10. And likewise if he ate second tithe (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:4).
(70) one who eats from a priest's meal offering. Which is burned entirely on the altar.
and likewise from anything that is entirely for the fires. For example, one who eats from the meat of a burnt offering and the sacrificial parts (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:1-3).
(71) one who eats from the meat of sin offerings that are burned, and likewise from anything that requires burning. Ibid. halakhah 3.
(72) one who slaughters the Passover offering while leaven is in his possession. Who has leaven in his possession at the time of slaughtering his Passover offering (Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:5).
(73) one who breaks a bone in it, whether on the first or the second. It is forbidden to break the bones of the Passover offering, in the first Passover and in the second Passover (ibid. 10:1).

(74) one who removes some of its meat outside its group. The Passover offering is eaten in one place by the group of people counted for it, and it is forbidden to remove it from the place designated for the group's eating (ibid. 9:1).
(75) one who eats of its meat outside its group. Meat that left its group is disqualified and forbidden (ibid. 9:2).
(76) one who eats of its meat raw or boiled. The Passover offering must be eaten roasted and not boiled or roasted insufficiently (ibid. 8:4).
(77) one who benefits from consecrated property deliberately. Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3.

(78) one who eats tevel from which ma'aser has not yet been separated, even poor man's tithe. In addition to terumot, one must separate from each crop the first tithe (for the Levite) and the second tithe (to be eaten in Jerusalem) or the poor man's tithe.
even though its terumot were separated. And there is already no death at the hands of Heaven for it (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:20).
(79) one who eats the flesh of a living animal whose case was concluded for stoning. For example, one with which a person had relations or which killed a person.
even if it was slaughtered. Even if it was slaughtered before being stoned and is not forbidden as a neveilah (ibid. 4:22).
(80) one who eats an impure animal. Ibid. 2:2.
(81-82) one who eats an impure bird, one who eats an impure fish. Ibid. 2:4.
(83) one who eats a flying swarming creature. Small flying creatures such as flies (ibid. 2:5).
(84) one who eats a land swarming creature. Small walking creatures (ibid. 2:6).
(85) one who eats a water swarming creature. Marine creatures not in the form of fish (ibid. 2:12).

(86) one who eats a creeping thing of the ground even if it does not reproduce. Worms and the like, which they thought were generated from mold and rot and not from the union of male and female (ibid. 2:13).
(87) one who eats worms in fruits after they emerged. But before they emerged, while still inside the detached fruit, one is not flogged for them (ibid. 2:14).
(88) one who eats neveilah. An animal that died without slaughter (ibid. 4:1).
(89) one who eats terefah. An animal with a wound or defect that makes it likely to die (ibid. 4:6).
(90) one who eats a limb from a living animal. A limb cut off from an animal while it was alive (ibid. 5:1).
(91) one who eats the sciatic nerve. The nerve on the hip socket in the animal's legs (ibid. 8:2).
(92-93) one who eats meat in milk, one who cooks meat in milk. Ibid. 9:1.
(94) one who eats from new grain before the omer is brought. Grain of the five species of grain that is forbidden to eat until the omer offering is brought on the 16th of Nisan (ibid. 10:3).
(95) one who eats orlah. Fruit of a tree in the first three years after its planting (ibid. 10:9).
(96) one who eats diverse kinds of the vineyard. Grapevines that grew together with grain or vegetables, all of which are forbidden to eat (ibid. 10:7).
(97) one who eats a mixture containing chametz on Passover. Food in which chametz is mixed (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 1:6; but for chametz itself one is liable to karet, as explained above halakhah 1).
(98) one who eats chametz after midday. On the eve of Passover (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 1:8).

(99) one who keeps chametz in his possession on Passover, such as one who leavened his dough. It is forbidden for a person to have chametz in his possession on Passover. However, he is liable to lashes only if he performed an act to have chametz in his possession (for example, he bought chametz or leavened dough with his hands during Passover), but one who left chametz with him during the days of Passover is not flogged, since this is a prohibition that involves no act (ibid. 1:3).
(100) one who drinks libation wine. Wine that was poured out for idolatry (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 11:1).

(101-103) a nazirite who ate of the grapevine... who became impure to a corpse. There are three kinds of prohibitions on a nazirite: eating things from grapes, cutting his hair, and impurity from the dead (Hilchot Nezirut 1:2).
(104-105) one who shaves the scall. Who removes the signs of tzara'at from his hair.
one who cuts off the signs of tzara'at. From tzara'at of the flesh.
or who burns them. Burns them (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 10:1).

(106) one who works in the valley where the heifer's neck was broken. When a slain person is found lying on the road and it is not known who struck him, the people of the nearest city bring a heifer and break its neck in a perennial stream. It is forbidden to work and sow the soil of this valley (Hilchot Rotzeach 10:9).
(107) one who sows the Land of Israel in the Sabbatical year. In a shemitah year (Hilchot Shemitah 1:2).
(108) one who prunes a tree in the Sabbatical year. Who cuts its branches to improve it (ibid.).
(109) one who reaps aftergrowth. Produce of the soil of the seventh year.
in the usual manner. As one reaps in all years (ibid. 4:1).
(110) one who harvests grapes in the usual manner. Who gathers the fruit of the tree (ibid. 4:22).

(111-113) one who sows in the Jubilee year... one who harvests in it in the usual manner. The fiftieth year after seven Sabbatical cycles is called the Jubilee, and everything forbidden in the Sabbatical year is forbidden in it (ibid. 10:15).
(114) one who finishes the corner of the field and does not give it to the poor. Who did not leave some of the crop for the poor but reaped his whole field (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 1:3).
(115) one who gathers gleanings and does not give them to the poor. Who collects for himself the stalks that fell during the reaping and does not leave them for the poor (ibid. 1:4).
(116) one who strips his vineyard and does not give it to the poor. Who takes the small clusters called 'olelot' and does not leave them for the poor (ibid. 1:5).
(117) one who gathers the fallen grapes of his vineyard and does not give them to the poor. Who collects single grapes that fell during the harvest and does not leave them for the poor (ibid.).
(118) one who takes the forgotten sheaf and does not give it to the poor. Who takes a bundle of cut stalks forgotten in the field and does not leave it for the poor (ibid.).
(119) one who takes the mother with the young and does not send away the mother. Who takes a bird with its chicks or eggs from the nest (Hilchot Shechitah 13:1).
(120) one who sows diverse kinds of seeds in the land. Who sows two kinds of seeds together. This prohibition applies only in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Kilayim 1:1-2).

(121) one who sows diverse kinds in the vineyard in the land. Who sows two kinds of grain or two kinds of vegetables, or grain and vegetables with grape seeds. This prohibition is from the Torah only in the Land of Israel (ibid. 5:1-2).

(122) one who grafts trees of diverse kinds anywhere. Who inserts a detached branch of a tree of one species into a tree of another species so that it joins with it. This prohibition is from the Torah even outside the Land (ibid. 1:5).
(123) one who crossbreeds diverse animals anywhere. Who breeds animals of two different species with each other (ibid. 9:1).
(124) one who drives diverse kinds anywhere. Who leads or works with two kinds of domestic or wild animals together (ibid. 9:7).
(125) one who muzzles an animal while it works anywhere. Who prevents it from eating while it works (Hilchot Sechirut 13:2).
(126) one who slaughters it and its offspring anywhere. Who slaughters an animal and its young on the same day (Hilchot Shechitah 12:1).

(127) one who takes a pledge from his fellow and does not return the pledge. One who enters the borrower's house to take a pledge or forcibly takes a pledge from the borrower transgresses a negative commandment, and it is a commandment to return the pledge. If he did not fulfill the positive commandment, he is flogged (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 3:4).

(128-129) one who takes a widow's pledge... one who takes as a pledge utensils used to prepare food and does not return them. It is forbidden to take a pledge from a widow, and it is forbidden to take from anyone as a pledge utensils used for preparing food, and if he took and did not return, he is flogged (ibid. halakhah 2).

(130) a conspiring witness who is not subject to payment. A false witness is punished with what he plotted to do to the one he testified against, and therefore when he plotted to make the other liable for money (or death), he is not flogged but pays (or is put to death). But when he testified in testimony that carries no liability for money or death, he is flogged (Hilchot Edut 20:8).
(131) one who strikes his fellow with a blow worth less than a peruta. But if it is worth a peruta, he is not flogged since he is liable to payments (Hilchot Chovel 5:3).

(132) a rebellious son on the first testimony. A rebellious son (who does not obey his father and mother and stole money from them and ate and drank with it gluttonously) is first brought to a court of three judges and flogged, and only if he later returns to his ways is he put to death (Hilchot Mamrim 7:7).
(133) one who spreads a bad name that was found false. Who claimed that his wife committed adultery during her betrothal and it became clear that he lied (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 3:1).
(134) one who curses his fellow by the Name. By one of the names of God (below 26:1).
(135) one who swears falsely. Hilchot Shevuot 1:3.

(136) one who swears in vain. Who swears about something known to be untrue, or about something known to everyone, or swears to nullify a commandment, or swears to do something he cannot do (ibid. halakhah 7).
(137) one who profanes his vow. Who transgressed his vow (Hilchot Nedarim 1:5).
(138) one who goes beyond the boundary on the Sabbath. Hilchot Shabbat 27:1.
(139) one who does work on a festival. Hilchot Shevitat Yom Tov 1:2.
(140) one who rounds the corner of his head. Who shaves one of the corners of the head (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:1).
(141) one who rounds the corner of his beard. Who shaves one of the corners of the beard in a destructive manner (ibid. 12:7).
(142) one who cuts himself for the dead. Who gashes his flesh out of mourning (ibid. 12:12).
(143) one who makes baldness on his head for the dead. Who removes his hair out of mourning (ibid. 12:15).
(144) one who writes a tattoo. Ibid. 12:11.
(145) one who wears shaatnez. A garment made of wool and linen together (Hilchot Kilayim 10:30).
(146) one who cuts down fruit trees in a destructive manner. Hilchot Melachim 6:8.
(147-148) a man who wore women's clothing, a woman who wore men's clothing. Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:10.
(149) a priest who became impure to a corpse. Hilchot Evel 3:1.

(150-152) a priest who betrothed a zonah, etc.. Who betrothed a woman who had relations with someone forbidden to her and became a zonah, or who betrothed a divorcee, or betrothed a challalah, a woman forbidden to the priesthood who had relations with a priest or who was born of a union forbidden to the priesthood.
and had relations with her. After the betrothal (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:2).
(153) and a high priest who had relations with a widow, even if he did not betroth her. Ibid. halakhah 3.
(154) one who remarries his divorced wife after she was betrothed. To another man (Hilchot Gerushin 11:12).

(155) one who marries a woman awaiting yibbum. A woman whose husband died without leaving children, and whose brother is obligated to enter into levirate marriage with her or to perform chalitzah, and until one of these is done she is forbidden to marry another (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:18).
(156) one who has relations with a kedeshah. A harlot; one who has a relation of harlotry without betrothal (Hilchot Ishut 1:4).
(157) a mamzer. One born of a union forbidden under penalty of karet.
who married an Israelite woman and had relations. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:2.
(158) one whose testicles are crushed. A man whose sexual organs were injured.
who married an Israelite woman and had relations. Ibid. 16:1.
(159) one who castrates a man, and likewise other males of animals, beasts, and birds. Ibid. 16:10.

(160) a rapist who divorced the woman he raped and did not take her back. The rapist is obligated to marry the woman he raped (if she desires), and is forbidden to divorce her. If he transgressed the prohibition and did not afterwards fulfill the positive commandment that she be his wife, he is flogged (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:7).

(161) one who spreads a bad name who divorced his wife and did not take her back. One who spreads a bad name about his wife (falsely claiming that she committed adultery while betrothed) is obligated to remain married to her forever (ibid. 3:4).
(162) one who approaches forbidden relatives in a manner of harlotry, etc.. For example, by embracing and kissing, even though he did not have relations (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:1-2).
(163) one who intermarries with gentiles. One who has relations with a gentile woman (ibid. 12:1).
(164-165) an Ammonite convert who married an Israelite woman and had relations, a Moabite convert, etc.. Converts from Ammon and Moab may not marry daughters of Israel (ibid. 12:18).
and they turned away their eyes. They diverted their eyes for a moment and did not see the act of killing itself.
and innocent and righteous. That there is a possibility that he is not the guilty one (as explained shortly).

this one saw him worship the sun and warned him, and this one saw him worship the moon and warned him. To testify in capital cases both witnesses must see him together commit the transgression (Hilchot Edut 4:1).
under duress. With no choice, being forced to transgress the prohibition.

even if he was commanded to be killed rather than transgress. That he was forced to transgress commandments for which he is obligated to give up his life rather than transgress (idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed; Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 5:2).

even though he profaned the Name, etc.. One who transgresses a prohibition for which he must give up his life and is not killed profanes the Name, but since he transgressed under duress he is not put to death (ibid. halakhah 4).
"and to the girl you shall do nothing". A betrothed girl who was raped is not put to death, and from this they learned for all who act under duress.
a man who was forced until he had relations with a forbidden relative, etc.. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:9.
for there is no erection except by intent. The organ does not become erect without the will of the one having relations, and therefore this is not considered duress.

she is exempt because her inclination overpowered her. The inclination took hold of her so that she could not master it, for a person's inclination and nature compel her to desire, and therefore she is considered under duress (see also Hilchot Ishut 24:19).
benefit. Advantage.

on one who became liable to a fine. For example, he injured his fellow and became liable to payments of damage, pain, healing, loss of time, and shame, some of which are defined as a fine (see also Hilchot Chovel 1:4).
to support him. To give him charity.
do not show deference. Do not honor.
so that the other's arguments not be silenced. For when he sees the judge honoring his opponent and receiving him graciously, he will think the judge's inclination is toward the other's favor.
he does not turn to one of them. To inquire after his welfare and converse with him.
how can I shame him. By holding him liable in judgment.

do not say, 'Since he is wicked and presumed to lie, and the other is presumed not to vary his speech, etc.'. Rather, as long as the case is not concluded, regard both of them as though they were liars (below 23:10).
one who delays the case. Who delays in ruling.
one who is arrogant in ruling. Who is confident in his knowledge and reasoning and does not hesitate to rule immediately.
and there is in the province someone greater than he in wisdom and he does not go and consult him. Rather he relies on a resemblance to a known law.
from arrogance. Pride.
for she has cast down many wounded: this is a student who has not reached the level to rule and rules. Who rules improperly and causes others to stumble into transgression.

and mighty are all her slain: this is one who has reached the level to rule and does not rule. Although he did not actively cause them to stumble, the result of his refusing to rule is that people stumble into transgression.
but if he knew that there is someone there fit to rule. And there is no need for him to rule as well (see above 3:10).
he prevents enmity. Of the litigants.
and robbery and a vain oath. If he errs and holds the innocent liable, or imposes an oath improperly.
and one who is arrogant in ruling is a fool, wicked, and haughty. See also Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:4.
and a student should not rule on a halakhah in front of his teacher. See also Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:3.
three parasangs. Twelve mil (about twelve kilometers).
corresponding to the camp of Israel. The length and width of the camp of Israel in the wilderness was twelve mil.
they conclude his case even for less than a peruta. Even if the amount of the claim fell below a peruta for various reasons.

and if he is an orphan, he transgresses three negative commandments. Regarding a convert who is also an orphan he transgresses three negative commandments, and regarding an orphan who is not a convert he transgresses only one negative commandment, as with any Israelite (Radbaz).
one should not speak at length while the other is told, 'Shorten your words'. So that his arguments not be silenced when he sees that the judge is patient toward his opponent and not toward him.
they say to the honored one, 'Either dress him, etc.'. So that they stand equally before the judge.
to what does this apply. That the litigants may be seated.
and what is the conclusion of a case, etc.. Below 22:9.
witnesses always stand. Even during deliberation.

they seat the scholar and say to the am ha'aretz, 'Sit,' etc.. The scholar is seated to honor him, and to equalize between them they tell the other also to sit. And if they gave him permission to sit, even though he did not sit, the judgment is considered just.

and a student should not come early when he has a case and sit before his teacher before whom he wants to be judged. When a student has a case being tried before his teacher, he is forbidden to come early to his teacher, so that it not appear that he came early to arrange his arguments before his teacher before his opponent arrives (see below halakhah 7, that a judge is forbidden to hear a litigant's words in the absence of his opponent).
to read. To study.
in order to remove dispute. On the part of people who would not be willing to stand.
and the case of a woman precedes the case of a man. Who is not a Torah scholar.
or not in the presence of his fellow. After his fellow had arrived, for example when he left.
hear between your brothers. That one must hear both litigants, each in the presence of the other.

you shall not bear a false report. For usually what is said in the absence of the other litigant is not honest and true, and when a judge hears only one side a false picture of the case may become fixed in his mind (Sefer HaMitzvot, Negative Commandment 281).
and included in this prohibition is a warning to one who accepts slander, etc.. All false and improper speech is included in this prohibition (ibid.).
the judge may not hear through an interpreter. When he does not understand the language of the litigants.
unless he knew, etc.. Where he understands the language but is not fluent in it and therefore cannot speak it, he is permitted to judge, but must appoint an interpreter to speak for him as needed.
and to repeat their arguments. To restate them.
as it is said, 'And the king said, etc.'. King Solomon himself repeated the arguments of the two women who came before him to be judged on the question of who was the mother whose son had died.
and justify the verdict in his heart, and then decide it. He must clarify the law thoroughly until he is sure of its justice, and only then rule.

that he not become an advocate for his words. That he not justify the words of one of the litigants (Kesef Mishneh, and see Rabbenu Chananel, Shevuot 30b). Some explain that if the judge is not at peace with his ruling, he should not justify his words with various pretexts (R. Y. Kafih based on Rashi there).

and he should not teach any of the litigants an argument at all. The judge rules on the basis of the litigants' arguments and is forbidden to intervene in their arguments and tell them how they should argue.
they do not accept one witness. Hilchot Edut 5:1.
and would that he admit and say that the witness testified truly. And the case would be decided on the basis of his admission.
until he argues and says, 'He is one witness,' etc.. That he denies the witness's words and argues that he is not believed because he is one witness, and then they accept his argument.
and a litigant wants to say it but does not know how to put his words together. He does not know how to formulate the argument.

he strains to save himself with a true argument, etc.. He tries to justify himself with an argument that appears true, and does not succeed because he is angry or lacks the understanding to say the matter properly.
to assist him slightly and to help him understand the beginning of the matter. To help him open his words so that he can present his argument well.
and he must deliberate on this matter at length. To weigh the matter and be careful with it.

like the court's advocates. The court's advocates are people who come with the authorization of a litigant and argue in his place, and thereby they in effect 'arrange' the judges (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 1:8). Here the prohibition for a judge is to be like them, by teaching the litigant to argue an argument, as above halakhah 10.
I do not engage with you. To be a judge in your case.
do not fear. Do not be afraid.
and if he was appointed over the public. To judge them.

he transgresses "do not fear any man". For the expression "do not fear" is also interpreted in the sense of gathering in words, that is, a student may not hold back his words and remain silent (Tosefta, Sanhedrin 1:8).
that he not seat an ignorant student before him. Who might mislead him.
what is a judgment that has peace with it. That is done by agreement and peace between the two sides.
compromise. Settlement.

what is a judgment that has righteousness with it? That is compromise. In making a compromise there is a combination of following the rules of law while also considering charity toward the liable party.
let the law pierce the mountain. Let him rule firmly according to the strict law.

they may go back and demand judgment until they perform a kinyan from both of them. For the compromise to be binding a kinyan sudar must be performed on it (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there), and if they did not perform a kinyan, even after they were told how much each must compromise, each of them can retract and demand that a judgment be made for them.
for two laymen who judged, their judgments are not judgments. Above 2:10.
asked. Requested.
one of the litigants to write him a ruling. And it is written for him (as explained above 6:6).

by their words so-and-so was acquitted. They write this way because this wording is accurate even where not all the judges agreed to acquit him, and on the other hand it reveals no secret (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 30a).
it is forbidden to join with him, as it is said, 'Distance yourself from a false matter'. One must distance oneself from sitting in judgment with a judge who is presumed to lie.
those expert in knowledge. Those expert in the laws.
they do not sit in judgment until they know with whom they are sitting. See also above 2:14.
and they do not sign on a document until they know who is signing with them. For if he signs with an unfit person, their testimony will also be disqualified.
and they do not enter a meal until they know who is reclining with them. So that they not recline in the company of ammei ha'aretz.
needless to say, to pervert the law. To take money in order to judge improperly.
but even to acquit the innocent and convict the guilty is forbidden. Even if the judge who takes the bribe does not intend to tilt the verdict in favor of the giver but to judge truly.
and just as the taker transgresses a negative commandment, so does the giver. For the giver causes the judge who takes to stumble into the prohibition of bribery.
as it is said, 'and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block'. From this the prohibition of causing people to stumble into transgression is learned (see Hilchot Rotzeach 12:14).

any judge who sits and magnifies his status in order to increase the pay of his attendants and scribes. Who is concerned to increase his importance, so that on that basis people will give his attendants and the scribes of the judges in his cases much money.
those who incline after gain. Who seeks money, even though this is not outright bribery.
a bribe of words. For example, flattering him with words or in another non-monetary way.
in a dugit. A small boat in which fish are caught.
and he had a case. That he wanted this judge to judge for him.
I am disqualified for you for judgment. Because of the help he gave him.
a feather. A plume.
a shawl. A kind of head covering.
to a sharecropper. A person who works the owner's field and shares the produce with him.

he brought early on Thursday because he had a case. For on that day the court sat in judgment and he wanted to be judged by him. He told him that since he had to come to him for judgment anyway, he brought his produce (see Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 105b).
who borrows. Who takes things on loan.
where the judge had nothing to lend. Of his own things to others.
that it not be an evident reward. That it not be apparent that he is receiving it as payment for judging, but that he receives payment because he is idle from his work.
give me someone who will work in my place until I judge for you. Hire a substitute for me.
only pay for idleness. See Piskei VeShitot.
it is forbidden for a judge to judge for one who loves him... or for one who hates him. Although he is valid to testify about them (Hilchot Edut 16:6).
his groomsman. One of his closest friends, such as those with him during the days of his wedding (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 3:5).
and if he did not know one of them. That he does not know either of them.
a sword placed on his neck and Gehenna open beneath him. That if he deviates from the line of law he will be punished.

God stands in the divine assembly and says, 'See,' etc.. From this it follows that the judge judges God's judgment, and stands before Him at the time of judgment and He will exact payment from him if he perverts the law.
and He will despoil the life of those who despoil them. He will take the lives of the judges who take money improperly.
and perhaps the judge will say, 'What have I to do with this trouble'. And will want to avoid judging for fear that he will not judge properly.

and 'He is with you in the matter of judgment': the judge has only what his eyes see. God will be with the judge who judges according to what appears to him, and therefore a judge who intends to judge according to the truth need not worry.

let the litigants always be before you as wicked ones. One must examine the litigants' claims thoroughly and treat both sides with suspicion as though both were presumed liars. And he should not rely on their claims even if one of them is presumed a liar and the other is upright (see above 20:5).
as righteous ones who have accepted the judgment upon themselves. Since they agreed to accept the ruling, even the one liable in the judgment is considered righteous.
and the matter is firm in his heart that it is so. That he is convinced of the correctness of the matter.
even though there is no clear proof there. For under the usual strict law, the judge must rule on the basis of witnesses and clear proof.
that a person became liable for an oath in court. On a claim brought against him, for example he admitted part of the claim and became liable for an oath by Torah law.
he is suspected regarding an oath. Of swearing falsely.

to reverse the oath onto his opponent, who swears and collects. Not to allow him to swear and be released from the claim, but to transfer the oath to the claimant, who swears and collects according to his claim.
even if a woman or a slave is trusted by him. Although they are disqualified from testifying, since he completely believes them, he must rely on them.

if there is a debt document against him to another, he should give to the one whose document is not flawed. When two creditors claim from this person and he can pay only one of them, he should prefer the claimant whose document is credible in his eyes.
he throws the document in his face and does not judge it at all. He does not consider the document at all, and does not adjudicate this claim.
that I have a deposit with so-and-so, who died without a will. And he has no proof with which he could recover his deposit from the dead man's heirs.
and he gave distinguishing marks. For example, he stated the weight of the deposit.

if the judge knows that this dead man was not presumed to own such an object, etc.. For example, it is a very valuable object that, in the judge's estimation, it is not fitting for this person to have (see also Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 6:4, where it is explained that the judge may rely only on his own estimation, and if he does not know the dead man he may not rely on others to testify to him about their estimation).

if so, why did the Torah require two witnesses. For he could judge on the basis of his own estimation, or on the word of one person whom he trusts, even if that person is disqualified from giving testimony.
are not as wise and discerning as is fitting. To rely on their own estimation.
that they not reverse an oath except on the basis of clear proof. For example, where there are witnesses that the claimant is suspected of swearing falsely (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 2:3).

and they should not impair a document and cause it to lose its presumption of validity through the testimony of a woman or a disqualified person. But one valid witness is believed to impair the document and to impose an oath (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1).
one does not take property from orphans except on the basis of clear proof. For example, witnesses who testified that he made the deposit with their father (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 6:4).
I will decide it, and the blame will hang on the neck of the witnesses. I will rule according to the words of the witnesses even though they are liars, and they will be punished for lying.
the collar. A chain hung on the neck of prisoners.
how should he proceed. When he suspects that the case is a fraud.

with the inquiry and examination used in capital cases. Although ordinarily one does not inquire and examine in monetary cases (Hilchot Edut 3:1), in order to establish the truth of the case one must inquire in every way possible.
and misled the witnesses. He led them astray.

for these matters are entrusted to the heart, and Scripture says, “for the judgment is God's”. For the Holy One, blessed be He, knows whether the judge's intention is to rule according to the truth (see Sma"a 15, note 11).
and to put to death one who is not liable to death. See also Hilchot Rotze'ach 2:4.
to make a fence around the Torah. For example, when there is a need to deter others.

there was an incident in which a man who had relations with his wife under a tree was flogged. Even though she was his wife and permitted to him, they gave him a rebellious-offender's flogging because he committed an act of lewdness, having relations in a public place (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:14).

and there was an incident of a man who rode a horse on the Sabbath in the days of the Greeks, and they brought him to court and stoned him. Even though the prohibition of riding on the Sabbath is only a rabbinic decree (Hilchot Shabbat 21:9).
and Shimon ben Shatach hanged eighty. Women who were sorceresses (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 6:4).
on one day in Ashkelon. Even though two people are not sentenced to death on one day, and women are not hanged (Mishnah Sanhedrin there; and see above 14:10, 15:6).
to a court in every place and at every time. Even judges outside the Land of Israel who are not ordained, and even at a time when capital cases are not tried.

a person with a bad reputation, about whom the people murmur that he commits forbidden sexual relations. A rumor spreads about him that he commits forbidden sexual relations, but there are no witnesses to it.
provided that the rumor is one that does not stop, as we have explained. That the rumor continued and spread for a day and a half or more without interruption (Hilchot Sotah 2:14).
and to strengthen the breach. To repair the cracks in the wall of the faith.

to excommunicate and to place under a ban. One in niddui behaves as a mourner, is not counted for matters requiring a quorum, and one may not come close to him. One under cherem is more severe, in that one also may not study with him (for the laws of niddui and cherem see Hilchot Talmud Torah chapter 7).
one liable to niddui. A person who is obligated to be placed in niddui.
