Curse Meroz. They cursed the city of Meroz, as stated in the Song of Deborah, because it did not come to help in the war; hence one must excommunicate (Babylonian Talmud, Mo'ed Katan 16a).
said the angel of the Lord. That one should tell the excommunicated person that the niddui was imposed on the word of a great man, the judge, who is like the angel of the Lord (ibid.).
curse bitterly. Place under a ban (ibid.).
because they did not come to the help of the Lord. This explains what the sin is, and hence one must publicize the sin (ibid.).
to bind the hands. To shackle, to tie the hands behind the back.

whether to death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment. The previous verse says that Ezra is given authority to appoint judges who will judge the people according to the laws of the Torah, and in this verse he is given authority to punish anyone who does not obey these laws in the ways mentioned here: to kill (“to death”), to pursue (“to banishment”), to declare property ownerless (“confiscation of goods”), and to imprison (“imprisonment”).

and in everything his actions should be for the sake of Heaven. With the intention of pursuing justice and increasing the honor of God, and not in order to take revenge on those judged or to be cruel to them.
and the dignity of people should not be light in his eyes. To punish them lightly.
a negative commandment of their words. A prohibition of the Sages (Hilchot Kilayim 10:29).
with authority. Control and haughtiness.
a parnas. An appointee.
therefore people feared him; he did not see any wise of heart. Because people were afraid of him, he did not see the son of a Torah scholar.
levity. Contempt.

and he should not step over the heads of the holy people. He should not walk about while everyone is seated (Rashi, Sanhedrin 7b). It may also be explained that he should not behave in a haughty way that looks like treading on their heads and being above them (see Yad Peshutah).
and he bears the burden of the community and their load like Moses our teacher. Similarly, the king is commanded to behave likewise (Hilchot Melachim 2:6).
and I commanded your judges. This is said in Moses our teacher's description of the process of appointing the judges of the people.
from the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
all the more so to eat, drink, and get drunk in front of many people. For these things cause those who see them to show great contempt (see Hilchot De'ot 5:2-3).
and at gatherings of ignoramuses. To eat, drink, and get drunk in a place where ignoramuses gather.
and at a feast of companions. A gathering of friends, a meal that is not a mitzvah meal.
woe to those judges who behaved so, to the disgrace of the Torah of Moses, whose laws they have shamed. For they represent the Torah and its laws, and their disgrace is its disgrace.
is believed like two. Like two witnesses.
regarding niddui. That one must excommunicate one who shames a Sage, who shames the court's messenger, or who refuses to come to judgment (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14).
he treated me with contempt. He showed contempt for me.
we excommunicate. We place in niddui.

but they do not write a pitcha against him until two come and testify that he refused to come. A pitcha is a writ of excommunication, and the excommunicated person must bear the cost of writing the document (below, halakhah 8). The court's messenger is believed like two as regards niddui, but not regarding the collection of money (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 112b).

and the court's messenger is not culpable for saying these things on account of slander. He does not violate the prohibition of slander if he reports what the litigant said about the judges or about him, or that he refuses to come to judgment.
so-and-so sent me, etc.. Such-and-such a judge summons you to judgment.
a pitcha of shamta. A writ of excommunication, where two have testified about it as above, halakhah 5.

until he says in the name of all three. A litigant is obligated to come only when three judges summon him to judgment. Even though here three judges did summon him, since he was summoned in the name of only one of the judges, he is not placed in niddui if he refused.
but on the known day on which the judges sit for judgment... as if he came in the name of all three. And he may be placed in niddui if he refuses to come.
and he pays the scribe's fee. He must bear the cost of writing the pitcha.
and when he comes they tear up the pitcha. But they do not tear up the pitcha before he comes, even if he said he agrees to come.
because he did not accept. He did not accept the verdict, for example he did not agree to pay what they held him liable for.

once he said, “I accept the judgment”. Even though he has not yet carried out the ruling and paid (for perhaps he has nothing to pay at present, so he should be released even though he has not yet paid).
in the city. In the town.

they set him a time, Monday and Thursday and Monday, etc.. They summon him for Monday; if he does not come they summon him again for Thursday, and if he does not come they summon him on the following Monday, and only the next day (Tuesday of the second week) do they write a pitcha against him.
they do not set a time. For judgment.
nor on the eve of the Sabbath. See also above 11:3.
they set it in Nisan to come after Nisan. That the summons to judgment is made in the month of Nisan, and the judgment will be after the month of Nisan.
because everyone is preoccupied on the eve of the Sabbath. And they might forget the summons.
and if he did not come, they place him in niddui the next evening. For presumably they informed him.
when it is not on the route he usually travels to the court's location. That the court is not on his way.

for they say, “his route passes the court, etc.”. The neighbors assume that since his route passes near the court, he presumably was already at the court and finished the case, so they do not inform him.
and so too if he did not come to the town until the next day. If it is not his practice to come on that day.
they do not rely on the neighbors. To tell him on the following day to come.
and he accepted the judgment, and they told him to pay, and he went and did not pay. He said he agrees to the ruling, but in practice he did not pay.
and if thirty days passed and he did not seek the lifting of his niddui. He did not ask to have the niddui lifted.

they place him under cherem. Cherem is more severe than niddui (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:5; there are cases in which one acts differently toward someone who does not seek the lifting of his niddui, depending on the circumstances of the case; see there halakhot 6-7 and Rabbi Kafih there).
Elohim. A term for judges.

one is the head of the Great Sanhedrin or the king. Both are called “nasi”: the king has supreme governing standing, and the head of the Sanhedrin has supreme Torah standing (Sefer ha-Mitzvot, negative commandment 316).
whoever curses an Israelite receives lashes. Even though there is no action involved, one receives lashes for it (above 18:2).
and why was “deaf” stated. For the prohibition applies to every person.
that even this one who does not hear and was not pained by this curse. And one might have thought that the prohibition of cursing is only because of the pain it causes one's fellow.
if he cursed a nasi he receives three. Because the nasi is also a judge.

he is liable on account of four names: three of an ordinary person and one on account of the father. There is a separate prohibition on a person cursing his father or mother (Hilchot Mamrim 5:1), so one who curses his father who is the nasi violates four prohibitions (though in practice he does not receive four sets of lashes, since one who curses his father and mother is liable to death, so if he was warned about death he does not receive lashes, and if he was warned about lashes he does not receive lashes for cursing his father and mother, since that falls under the warning of a death penalty by the court; see Or Sameach).
take care and guard yourself well. From this we learn that a person is obligated to take care not to harm himself.
with one of the Names. Of the Holy One, blessed be He (for the list of the Names see Hilchot Yesodei ha-Torah 6:2).
with a epithet. A description by which the Holy One, blessed be He, is referred to, though it is not one of the holy Names.

and “cursed” includes an oath, a curse, and niddui. The word “arur” (cursed) is considered a curse, and one who curses with it (for example, saying “So-and-so is cursed to God”) receives lashes. It also serves as an oath (for example, saying “Cursed to God be whoever eats such-and-such,” and if he eats it he has sworn falsely; Hilchot Shevuot 2:2), and it can also serve as the wording with which one places in niddui a person liable to niddui (Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:2).
like all others liable for negative commandments. Above 16:4.
for the curse came from the general meaning of the words. That from the meaning of his words it follows that the person will be cursed.
if he insulted a Torah scholar, they place him in niddui. And they also fine him to give the Sage he shamed a litra of gold (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:12, Hilchot Chovel 3:5).
and if the judges wish to give him a rebellious-offender's flogging. In addition to niddui (Sma"a 27, note 9; see there for another explanation).
the elder. The Sage.
the judges act in the matter as the hour requires. The judges may punish even one who is not liable to punishment, in order to fence in and strengthen what needs strengthening (above 24:4).

according to the one who insults and the one who is insulted. A curse against a distinguished person, or by a distinguished person, is more serious than a curse by or against a person who is not distinguished.
for a judge or a nasi may forgo his own honor. He is permitted to if he wishes (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:6).
he cannot forgo the curse against him. In any case one who cursed him is flogged, on account of cursing a judge or also cursing a nasi.
who became liable to niddui because he flouted the court. For he showed contempt and rebelled against the judges (see above 25:5 ff.).
since the people have grown lax in the matter, they need to strengthen and punish as seems fit to them. And they may not forgo.
in gentile law. According to gentile law.
and in their courts. Their courts of law (even if they judge there by Jewish law).
“before them,” and not before gentiles. That one must be judged specifically before Jewish judges, even if a gentile court judges according to Jewish law.

“before them,” and not before laymen. That one must be judged specifically before qualified judges who judge by Jewish law, and not before laymen, who do not judge according to the law of the Torah but according to gentile law (Yad Peshutah).
the gentiles' hand was strong. And their judges can extract money even from those who refuse and do not obey the judgment.
